steps.observation: You have 10 seconds. Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
The foghorn failed the night the ship disappeared.

Elias, the lighthouse keeper, stood alone in the lantern room, watching the beam sweep a pale arc across the black sea. For forty-two years, he had tended this light: trimming the wick, polishing the lens, winding the clockwork so the beacon would never falter.

Tonight, the mechanism jammed.

He heard it before he saw it: a strained, grinding hesitation in the gears. The beam paused, blinked, then stuttered out. Darkness rushed in like water through a broken hull.

Elias’s hands moved by memory. He crossed the narrow room, freed the snagged chain with a twist and a curse, and struck the backup lantern with a match. Flame leapt, glass flared, but in the seconds of darkness he heard something out in the fog—a horn, too close, too frantic.

He cranked the emergency lamp to life and threw the shutters wide. Light slashed the mist.

There, through the swirling gray, a freighter’s silhouette loomed, impossibly near the jagged teeth of the reef. He held his breath as the ship listed, turning—too slow, too slow—its bow scraping unseen stone. A sound like the world tearing itself in half rolled up to the tower.

The ship did not sink.

Instead, it leaned, caught in a cradle of rock, bleeding cargo into the waves. Elias watched until the shouting on deck faded into the distance and the ship became another black shape against a blacker sea. Only when the rescue cutters’ lights approached did he finally exhale and sit down on the cold floor.

The report arrived months later. The company blamed outdated charts. The captain blamed the fog. No one blamed the moment the light went out.

But Elias did.

He kept the letter folded in his pocket after that, a stiff white weight against his heart. Each night, he checked the gears three times instead of two. He polished the lens until it shone like a second moon. When the fog rolled in, he stayed awake until dawn, fingers wrapped around the railing as if he could hold the whole coastline steady.

Years passed. New ships with better instruments traced neat lines on digital maps and barely glanced at the old lighthouse. The town council talked of automation. “The world doesn’t need keepers anymore,” they said.

On his last night, Elias climbed the spiral stairs slower than before, his knees complaining at every turn. The lantern room smelled of oil and salt and all his years. He set the clockwork one final time and watched the beam sweep out to sea.

Nothing answered. No horn, no light, just the slow breathing of the waves.

He stood there until the clock chimed midnight, then spoke aloud to the empty room.

“You’re on your own now,” he told the light. “But then, you always were. I was only the one who stayed to watch.”

He descended the stairs, took his coat from its hook, and stepped out into the predawn dark. Behind him, the beam turned, steady and indifferent, cutting its patient path through the fog—still warning, still waiting—for ships that might never again know there had once been a keeper who believed, fiercely, that being unseen did not make a duty small.
